topic: Multi-intent task decomposition for LLM tool and skill routing
name: RouteLLM
description: RouteLLM (arXiv:2406.18665, 'Learning to Route LLMs with Preference Data', Isaac Ong et al., LMSYS / UC Berkeley, ICLR 2025) is a framework for binary strong-vs-weak LLM routing trained on preference data. For each query it predicts the probability that a strong (high-quality, high-cost) model will outperform a weak (cheaper) model — the strong-model win rate — and applies a user-set threshold alpha: win rate >= alpha routes to the strong model, else to the weak model. It implements four router types (matrix factorization, BERT classifier, causal-LLM classifier, similarity-weighted/SW Elo ranking) trained on Chatbot Arena human preference labels augmented with LLM-judge pairwise labels. With GPT-4 Turbo (strong) and Mixtral 8x7B (weak), matrix factorization reaches 95% of GPT-4 performance at 26% GPT-4 calls (~48% cheaper than random; with augmentation, 14% calls / ~75% cheaper); cost reductions of >85% (MT Bench), 45% (MMLU), 35% (GSM8K) at 95% GPT-4 quality. Routers generalize to unseen pairs (Claude 3 Opus / Llama 3 8B) without retraining and match commercial routers (Martian, Unify) at >40% lower cost. Routing overhead is <=0.4% of generation cost. It is not multi-intent decomposition, but it is the canonical reference for classifier-gate design and the latency/cost trade-off framing.
decomposition_method: None — RouteLLM does not decompose prompts. Each query is treated as a single unit and classified to decide which model handles it. No sub-task splitting. [uncertain]
decomposition_granularity: Not applicable — no sub-tasks. The routed unit is the whole query / single chat request. [uncertain]
ordering_strategy: Not applicable — a single binary routing decision per query; no multi-step ordering or DAG. [uncertain]
decomposition_validation: Not applicable to decomposition (none performed). The analogous quality control is calibration of the predicted strong-win probability against a threshold alpha, validated empirically by cost-vs-quality curves (PGR / call-performance threshold metrics) on held-out benchmarks. [uncertain]
hierarchy_depth: flat — one binary decision (strong vs weak) per query; no hierarchy. (Can be chained into a cascade conceptually, but the framework's contribution is the flat binary gate.)
router_type: single-label binary classifier (strong vs weak). Realized four ways: (1) matrix factorization over preference data (best performer), (2) BERT text classifier with a logistic head, (3) causal-LLM classifier (e.g., Llama 3 8B) predicting win probability via next-token, (4) SW (similarity-weighted) Elo ranking weighting Arena votes by prompt similarity. All output a continuous strong-win probability thresholded by alpha.
routing_model: Separate trained router (not necessarily the served LLM): matrix-factorization win predictor, a fine-tuned BERT classifier, a causal-LLM classifier, or a similarity-weighted Elo scorer. Trained on Chatbot Arena human preference data plus LLM-judge-augmented pairwise labels. Embedding/similarity (SW), learned classifiers (BERT/causal-LLM), and low-rank factorization (MF) all represented.
handles_ambiguity: threshold-based best-effort. Borderline queries (win rate near alpha) are resolved purely by the continuous probability vs the alpha cutoff — higher alpha sends more to the weak model (cheaper), lower alpha more to strong (better). No clarification request, no abstain, no parallel dispatch, no POMDP. The user tunes alpha to set the operating point on the cost-quality curve. [uncertain]
fallback_behavior: binary fallthrough to the weak (or strong) model — there is no 'no model covers this' case because exactly two endpoints always exist; the gate simply picks one. Effectively routes to the general LLM (weak by default unless win rate >= alpha). No error/abort, human escalation, or re-decomposition. [uncertain]
skill_pool_scale_and_retrieval: Not applicable in the skill sense — the candidate pool is exactly two models (strong, weak), not a large skill/tool registry. No embedding retrieval or top-k over many skills; scaling beyond two models is out of scope (extension to >2 / cascades noted as future/related work). [uncertain]
router_agent_asymmetry: Not applicable — no skill text / agent asymmetry. Both models receive the same query; the router sees only the query (and learned preference structure) to decide. [uncertain]
execution_pattern: Not a multi-task executor — a single chosen model answers each query (ReAct-style single forward pass per query). The router is a drop-in OpenAI-compatible client/server that forwards to one backend. No fan-out. [uncertain]
parallel_vs_concurrent: Not applicable — exactly one model executes per query; no parallel or concurrent multi-call execution. [uncertain]
dependency_detection: Not applicable — no sub-tasks, so no dependency analysis. [uncertain]
result_aggregation: Not applicable — the single selected model's output is the final response; no merging of multiple sub-results. [uncertain]
mid_chain_feedback: none — the routing decision is made once per query upfront with no mid-chain re-planning or re-routing based on partial results. [uncertain]
benchmark_name: MT Bench (160 open-ended questions, LLM-as-judge), MMLU (14,042 questions / 57 subjects), and GSM8K (1,000+ grade-school math). Evaluated routing GPT-4 Turbo (strong) vs Mixtral 8x7B (weak), with cross-pair generalization tested on Claude 3 Opus / Llama 3 8B.
multi_intent_coverage: Single-intent. Benchmarks are single-query tasks; no compound/multi-intent parallel-vs-sequential categories. The axis evaluated is query difficulty (does it need the strong model), not multi-intent composition. [uncertain]
accuracy_metric: outcome-based cost-quality curves: benchmark task accuracy/score (MMLU/GSM8K correctness, MT Bench LLM-judge score) plotted against fraction of strong-model calls (cost). Headline metrics include Performance-Gap-Recovered / Call-Performance-Threshold (e.g., calls needed to reach 95% of GPT-4 performance) and % cost reduction vs a random-routing baseline. Quantitatively, matrix factorization reaches 95% GPT-4 performance at 26% GPT-4 calls (~48% cheaper than random; 14% calls / ~75% cheaper with augmented data). Routing quality is judged by resulting answer quality at a cost level, not routing exact-match.
clarification_capability: Not measured. RouteLLM does not model when-to-ask vs when-to-answer and generates no clarification questions; it is a pure binary model-selection gate. [uncertain]
process_vs_outcome_eval: outcome-only — scored on final benchmark answers/judge scores at given cost; no intermediate process supervision.
eval_stability: Mixed/reproducible: MT Bench uses precomputed judgements for the model pair, and MMLU/GSM8K are computed via SGLang over fixed datasets, so the routing eval itself is reproducible; underlying numbers depend on the served model versions (live commercial APIs like GPT-4 Turbo can drift). Code, datasets, and trained routers are released for reproduction. [uncertain]
integration_pattern: standalone service / drop-in middleware: an OpenAI-compatible server or a drop-in replacement for the OpenAI client that intercepts each request and forwards to the strong or weak backend. Application-layer; not pushed into the inference engine.
routing_layer: application-layer — RouteLLM sits between the application and the model backends as an OpenAI-compatible router; it is not an inference-engine/gateway-layer (ext_proc) component. [uncertain]
latency_overhead: Very low. The router adds at most ~0.4% to generation cost for the most expensive router (SW ranking); lightweight classifiers (BERT/MF) add negligible latency. A single extra inference (the router) before forwarding to one model; no multi-round-trip planning.
online_adaptation: static — routers are trained offline on preference data and deployed with a fixed alpha threshold (the operating point is user-tunable but not auto-adapted). No production-feedback bandit/RL loop in the published framework; generalization to new pairs is achieved without retraining rather than via online learning. [uncertain]
adoption: open-source (with code, datasets, and trained models on GitHub lm-sys/RouteLLM and Hugging Face under LMSYS/RouteLLM orgs); research paper at ICLR 2025 (UC Berkeley / LMSYS). Widely used/forked as a reference framework and benchmarked against commercial routers (Martian, Unify AI); usable as a production OpenAI-compatible server, though it is primarily a research/reference framework rather than a vendor commercial API.
